item.title: Seventy-nine complete Gr 8 national exam at Sorovi primary
item.description: Sorovi Primary School, one of the top-performing primary schools in Oro Province, has successfully completed the 2026 National Grade 8 Examinations for its 79 students. Head Teacher Mrs. Yula Cimon confirmed this when addressing parents, students, and teachers during a small closing program held today to mark the end of the examination week.
item.content:encoded:
Sorovi Primary School, one of the top-performing primary schools in Oro Province, has successfully completed the 2026 National Grade 8 Examinations for its 79 students.

Head Teacher Mrs. Yula Cimon confirmed this when addressing parents, students, and teachers during a small closing program held today to mark the end of the examination week.

Mrs. Cimon said despite the challenges of El Niño and ‘Don’t Care’ activities affecting the province, the school successfully delivered both the Grade 8 National Examinations and the Grade 6 Benchmark Examinations simultaneously.

“God has protected the school, students and teachers to date, and the Grade 8 National Exams were conducted peacefully,” Mrs. Cimon said.

She extended her gratitude to the external and internal invigilators from Resurrection Primary School, Popondetta Primary School and Sorovi Primary School for their tireless commitment over the last four days.

The closing program included speeches from the BOM Chairman, external invigilators, teachers and parents, followed by a token of appreciation (Bondo) from the Grade 8 parents.

item.title: K12.5 million for El Nino relief in WHP
item.description: Western Highlands Province has received K12.5 million from the National Government for El Nino preparedness and response, but Provincial Administrator Joseph Iri Mangbil says the funding falls short of what the province needs to protect its people from the prolonged disaster. Mr. Mangbil says the Western Highlands Provincial Administration initially submitted a funding request of K21.7 million to
item.content:encoded:
Western Highlands Province has received K12.5 million from the National Government for El Nino preparedness and response, but Provincial Administrator Joseph Iri Mangbil says the funding falls short of what the province needs to protect its people from the prolonged disaster.

Mr. Mangbil says the Western Highlands Provincial Administration initially submitted a funding request of K21.7 million to the responsible national government department following an assessment of the province's needs.

However, only K12.5 million was approved, leaving the province to manage the El Nino situation with significantly less than it had requested.

The funding has been allocated to the four districts, with each receiving K2.5 million to implement their respective preparedness and response plans.

Mangbil adds Western Highlands faces a major challenge because of its population of about 700,000 people, which continues to grow as people migrate into the province from other parts of the Highlands.

He also adds the growing population will place additional pressure on available resources as authorities work to respond to the effects of El Nino.

“With our population of about 700,000 people, including those coming into the province from other Highlands provinces, responding to this El Nino situation will be a major challenge.”

Despite the funding shortfall, Mangbil stress public servants must not become complacent but should step up their efforts to ensure assistance reaches the people who need it.

He has reminded officers at all levels of government to remain committed to their duties and carry out their responsibilities effectively during this period of national disaster.

The Western Highlands Provincial Government will also contribute K500,000 to support district-level preparedness and response activities, in addition to the national funding.

The contribution from the provincial government is expected to be shared among the four districts, although the exact allocation to each district has yet to be confirmed.

The Chair of the Provincial Disaster Committee has also urged public servants to exercise patience, fairness and impartiality when dealing with communities affected by the disaster.

He says the effects of El Nino can create anxiety among the people, making it important for government officers to respond wisely and professionally, even when they face difficult situations.

He emphasises on cooperation, responsible leadership and proper management of available funds will be critical to helping Western Highlands communities cope with the prolonged El Nino conditions.

item.title: AI linear accelerator for POM Gen cancer patients
item.description: Cancer patients will soon receive pin-point precision treatment with Papua New Guinea's first AI-powered Linear Accelerator installed at the Port Moresby General Hospital Comprehensive Cancer Center. The Elekta Linear Accelerator from the United States is housed inside Bunker One, a full concrete structure with walls about 1.5 meters thick designed to safely contain radiation.
item.content:encoded:
Cancer patients will soon receive pin-point precision treatment with Papua New Guinea's first AI-powered Linear Accelerator installed at the Port Moresby General Hospital Comprehensive Cancer Center.

The Elekta Linear Accelerator from the United States is housed inside Bunker One, a full concrete structure with walls about 1.5 meters thick designed to safely contain radiation.

Chief Executive Officer of PomGen, Dr. Paki Molumi, said this is the first of its kind in the country, and a major upgrade from the old cobalt source machine in Lae.

"Radiotherapy machine, it's a linear accelerator from Elekta. Compare this to the one in Lae, it's a cobalt source. The thing about radiotherapy machines, if it's cobalt, it's going to burn your skin. It will burn your muscles all the way to get into the target.

Whereas this latest machine, it subtracts everything and only targets the cancer. Precisely, to the point of a pin. We are so lucky we are building this at a time of the AI age. Machines now have inbuilt AI to assist technicians," Dr. Molumi said.

Unlike the cobalt source which releases continuous radiation, the linear accelerator generates radiation on demand by electricity when patients are being treated.

Bunker Two will house a bigger TrueBeam machine, another version of Elekta to complement the first machine and treat different types of cancers depending on depth – neck, abdomen and other deep-seated organs.

According to Dr. Molumi, the radiation oncologist will decide which bunker a patient goes to, adding that the second machine is yet to be procured, with funding hoped for in the 2027 Budget.

For safety, bunkers are fitted with laser beams that pick-up movement and automatically shut down the machine if someone enters during radiation. Operators monitor patients from a shielded monitoring station with computers and cameras.

To make patients feel at home, Dr. Molumi said sterile walls will be covered with murals with PNG cultural designs.

He explained that the treatment workflow is linked, cancer is mapped out and programmed in the Planning CT room, and that information is fed into the linear accelerator to apply treatment directly to the planned field.

After treatment, response will be monitored in nuclear medicine through (Positron Emission Tomography) or PET Scan and Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT or CT) machines.

A SPECT/CT machine is a hybrid imaging system that combines SPECT with X‑ray Computed Tomography (CT) to provide both functional and anatomical imaging in a single scan.

Patients are injected with radioactive material with a half-life of 3-4 hours and kept in uptake rooms before scanning. The scan shows at cellular level whether chemotherapy or radiotherapy is curing the patient.

"After treatment is done, we will need to monitor at molecular level, because you don't know whether your radiotherapy or chemotherapy is actually curing this patient. That's where you get a PET scan. You can actually see the function at cellular level, whether treatment is responding.

Then you can increase dose, reduce dose, or look for other ways," Dr. Molumi explained.

The facility will be able to treat 30 to 60 patients per day when both machines are running.

item.title: WHP priorities water and food
item.description: Western Highlands Province is prioritising access to clean drinking water and food supplies as the effects of El Nino continue to threaten communities in the province. With rivers and creeks drying up, traditional food sources declining and local markets running short of produce, the provincial disaster committee says providing water and food must be the first priority in the ongoing response.
item.content:encoded:
Western Highlands Province is prioritising access to clean drinking water and food supplies as the effects of El Nino continue to threaten communities in the province.

With rivers and creeks drying up, traditional food sources declining and local markets running short of produce, the provincial disaster committee says providing water and food must be the first priority in the ongoing response.

Western Highlands Provincial Administrator and Provincial Disaster Committee Chairman, Joseph Mangbil, says the immediate concern is ensuring people have access to their basic necessities before addressing other impacts of the prolonged dry conditions.

"First and foremost, we have to look at the people's water sources, which are now running short or drying up, and their food supply.

"Our rivers and creeks have dried up, food sources are also drying up, and markets are becoming empty. We must take proactive steps to provide water and food for our people during this time," stressed Mangbil.

Mangbil says the provincial administration has held discussions with several supermarkets in town on how rice supplies could be delivered to affected communities.

However, he says accurate information from the districts and communities is critical to ensuring food reaches the people who need it most.

He has urged responsible officers to act quickly and provide the necessary data to support the distribution of food rations in the province.

The Provincial Disaster Chairman adds now that El Nino funding has reached the province and the four districts, district administrations must move from planning to implementation.

He stressed districts need to identify the most affected communities, organise food rationing and establish reliable water access points.

These may include water tanks and bore-water systems installed in accessible communal locations such as schools, marketplaces and ples singsing areas, allowing people from surrounding communities to collect water.

Mangbil iterate that the response must be practical and reach people at the community level, particularly those whose normal sources of drinking water and food have been affected by the dry conditions.

He has reiterated that securing food and water supplies remains the province's immediate priority.

Other concerns, including health services and possible school closures, will be addressed as part of the wider El Nino response.

For now, Mangbil says the focus is on ensuring communities have access to the two essentials they need most to get through the dry period: safe drinking water and food.

item.title: PMGH comprehensive cancer center phase 3 nears commissioning
item.description: Papua New Guinea's first Comprehensive Cancer Center at the Port Moresby General Hospital will commence chemotherapy and radiotherapy services before the end of this year, with Phase Three of the project set for commissioning. Chief Executive Officer of PomGen, Dr. Paki Molumi, said the facility will be the main cancer center for the country and has been designed as a one-stop-shop cancer center.
item.content:encoded:
Papua New Guinea's first Comprehensive Cancer Center at the Port Moresby General Hospital will commence chemotherapy and radiotherapy services before the end of this year, with Phase Three of the project set for commissioning.

Chief Executive Officer of PomGen, Dr. Paki Molumi, said the facility will be the main cancer center for the country and has been designed as a one-stop-shop cancer center.

The K300-million project has been split into phases due to lack of bulk government funding.

He said for Phase One, the two bunkers are completed, while phase two main structures are also completed and phase three’s Engineering and fit-out of the ground floor is now almost complete.

Dr. Molumi said Phase Three is the ground floor where key services will be provided.

"This will be the main cancer center for the country. Because of lack of funding, we split into phases. So on this floor we will be providing chemotherapy, radiotherapy in two bunkers, brachytherapy for cervical cancer, planning CT and nuclear medicine. On the upper floors will be for radio-iodine, immunotherapy, gene therapy. So we want to make thisa one-stop-shop cancer center," Dr. Molumi said.

On the ground floor, chemotherapy services currently provided at the main hospital will be moved to the new facility, along with radiotherapy in two bunkers, brachytherapy unit for cervical cancer, planning CT and nuclear medicine department.

The upper floors, to be fitted out from 2027 to 2030, will cater for radio-iodine treatment, immunotherapy, gene therapy, bone marrow transplant for leukemias, molecular lab, immunohistochemistry, histopathology and research facilities.

Dr. Molumi clarified that the center is a treatment facility, not an admission facility.

He said Provincial Health Authorities (PHAs) around the country must diagnose patients, perform required surgery, and have patients ready before referral to the cancer center for chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

After treatment, monitoring will be done at molecular level via (Positron Emission Tomography) or PET scan in the nuclear medicine department to assess response.

The center plans to commission the ground floor while fit-outs of upper floors continue, to avoid waiting until 2030 for the entire facility.

item.title: Multimillion road contract
item.description: The people of Bogia and surrounding communities in Madang Province area are set to benefit from improved road access, following the signing of a multi – million kina contract, today. Governor General Sir Bob Dadae executed the 77million kina road contract between the Department of Works and Highways and Contractor Dekenai Construction Limited.
item.content:encoded:
The people of Bogia and surrounding communities in Madang Province area are set to benefit from improved road access, following the signing of a multi – million kina contract, today.

Governor General Sir Bob Dadae executed the 77million kina road contract between the Department of Works and Highways and Contractor Dekenai Construction Limited.

The signing was witnessed by Madang Governor Ramsey Pariwa and Bogia MP Robert Naguri.

The multi- million-kina contract covers the upgrading and sealing of 20 kilometers of the Madang coastal road from Nimbia to Bunapas.

Project is being funded under the government’s signature Connect PNG programe, specifically for the Momase Corridor.

Department of Works Secretary Gibson Holemba thanked the government for its continued funding of the program, saying improved road connectivity is vital for service delivery and economic development.

Madang Governor Pariwa said the road upgrade will open up economic opportunities for locals and neighboring East Sepik Province.

ICT Minister and Local MP Robert Naguri says he is proud that the long – awaited road upgrade and sealing would finally take place.

The 20 year Connect PNG initiative, is aimed at connecting key economic corridors including the Momase corridor linking Morobe, Madang, East Sepik and West Sepik.

item.title: To’o: Humbled to play in PNG
item.description: Playing international rugby league in Papua New Guinea is something many rugby league players anticipate. Whether you’re Australian, Kiwi, English, Samoan, Tongan, Fijian, Cook Islander, French or Lebanese, the passionate Papua New Guinean rugby league fan is unique.
item.content:encoded:
Playing international rugby league in Papua New Guinea is something many rugby league players anticipate.

Whether you’re Australian, Kiwi, English, Samoan, Tongan, Fijian, Cook Islander, French or Lebanese, the passionate Papua New Guinean rugby league fan is unique.

You find them no where else in the world, only in Papua New Guinea, a nation that calls rugby league its national sport.

Playing in front of passionate rugby league fans who support their team [PNG Kumuls] and also cheer on their favorite players playing against them is something many NRL and Super League stars anticipate when they play in PNG.

Samoan International, New South Wales Blues, Penrith Panthers and PNG Chiefs 2028 bound Brian To’o is keen on ticking that box come Saturday, when he runs out with Toa Samoa to face the PNG Kumuls.

After touching down in Port Moresby yesterday, the four-time NRL premiership winner said he is humbled to play in front of passionate fans.

“If I have to put down to one word, I would say beautiful,” To’o said

“Beautiful place, and I am very blessed and honored to be here. I am very grateful to be amongst the people of PNG and the Samoan community here.”

“Given that we will be playing in that special stadium [Santos NFS], I know that from past games I’ve watched.”

“You can see how much it means to the people, and how much they really adore the sport.”

“The only thing I can do to honor them is putting up my best performance this week against the brothers from the Kumuls.”

Despite having way more NRL players than the Kumuls, To’o said they won’t be taking the Kumuls lightly.

“They are a massive team, you can see that by the purpose they have when they play for their country.”

“They put up a massive performance against Lebanon last week and it is obviously going to be a massive challenge for us and we just have to be prepared to bring that intensity.”

item.title: Mangbil calls for accountability in El Nino response
item.description: Western Highlands Provincial Administrator and Chairman of the Provincial Disaster Committee, Joseph Iri Mangbil, has called on district administrators and finance managers to ensure transparency, accountability and proper use of disaster funds in responding to the El Nino situation. Mr. Mangbil made the call during an urgent provincial El Nino coordination meeting attended by district administrat
item.content:encoded:
Western Highlands Provincial Administrator and Chairman of the Provincial Disaster Committee, Joseph Iri Mangbil, has called on district administrators and finance managers to ensure transparency, accountability and proper use of disaster funds in responding to the El Nino situation.

Mr. Mangbil made the call during an urgent provincial El Nino coordination meeting attended by district administrators, district finance managers, LLG managers and the Provincial Finance Manager, police, electoral commission and international partners like UNDP, UNICEF, DFAT earlier this week.

The meeting discussed situational reports from the four districts, district El Nino response plans, financial arrangements, accountability and coordination of the provincial response.

Mangbil acknowledged that the K2.5 million allocated to each district for disaster response was insufficient to meet all the needs of communities affected by the El Nino situation.

However, he stressed that the limited funding made needs proper financial management, timely implementation and accountability.

“Honesty, transparency and accountability will play a major role at this crucial time. We need to work together to deliver services and support our people.”

The Provincial Disaster Chairman urged district authorities to manage the available funds responsibly and ensure that assistance reached the intended communities without unnecessary delays.

He said the provincial government, districts, local-level governments and relevant agencies must work together to coordinate their response and address the challenges facing the people.

" We will not engage casuals to do our work. We have to be responsible public servants and carry our work with due diligent so that our people must not be affected by this prolong Elnino," said Mr. Mangbil.

He also emphasised the importance of time management, calling on responsible officers to act promptly rather than allow delays to affect the delivery of essential assistance.

With communities facing the effects of El Nino, Mangbil said cooperation and responsible leadership were necessary to ensure that the limited resources available were used effectively.

He called on the district administrations and finance managers to take their responsibilities seriously and ensure that financial decisions and response activities were properly managed and accounted for.

The urgent meeting forms part of the province's efforts to coordinate district-level response plans and establish appropriate financial and administrative arrangements to address the El Nino situation in Western Highlands Province.

item.title: Kupo range fresh produce supplies to farmers
item.description: While much of Simbu continues to feel the bite of the El Nino drought, the Kupo Range Fresh produce is planting hope by distributing seedlings, tools and farming materials to its 200 registered farmers and seven cluster groups from Kundiawa-Gembogl, Kerowagi and Gumine districts yesterday.
